stories.headline: France deploys 70,000 security personnel ahead of new protests after a week of riots

sources.body:
France is on high alert ahead of a new day of nationwide protests on Saturday, a week after the country saw some of its worst unrest in decades.

Sweeping restrictions have been imposed on demonstrations across France but hundreds of thousands of protesters are still expected to gather in Paris and elsewhere for a second round of protests organised by students, trade unions and wider anti-government groups.

The interior ministry has said it will deploy 70,000 police officers, ramping up the security presence in French cities, after the government was accused by opposition parties of failing to foresee the scale of the unrest on 17 October.

"We will not let anything go unchallenged," said Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez.

"We will be uncompromising with the vandals, with the looters, and all those who commit acts of violence," he added, explaining that separate from the planned protests, numerous calls for violence had been seen on social media from the "far left and radical extreme left".

Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings in recent days.

President Emmanuel Macron met high-school students' representatives on Friday ahead of Saturday's protests, and although they said he had made clear commitments to them, they said students should "continue to mobilise".

Macron decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted to take place on Saturday, and several key cities including Lyon, Nice and Montpellier have gone further by announcing blanket bans on gatherings .

Official announcements appear to have done little to deter organisers, with hundreds of large and small demonstrations planned across France.

After a week in which some cities have lived under partial curfews - including areas of the capital - there is an inconsistent picture across France's cities as to what level of protest will be permitted by authorities.

While some mayors have pressed ahead with broad bans, others have agreed to allow demonstrations registered with authorities - for example, in Marseille, a previous order barring all protests was swiftly reversed to allow a trade union-organised march to go ahead.

In Paris, a march organised by the student trade union and supported by labour groups has been ordered to stick to a route which does not go through the city centre - though preparations for unrest in some of the city's most recognisable areas are under way regardless.

The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums will all be closed on Saturday, a scheduled home match for football team PSG has been moved to Monday, and some businesses have boarded up their windows in anticipation of further looting.

In a sign of how a student-led protest movement expanded to become a wider anti-government outpouring, protesters associated with a revived gilet jaunes (yellow-vest) movement could be out in force across France on Saturday.

The protest movement, which has attracted support from left and right, led huge disruptive demonstrations during Macron's first term in office.
sources.headline: France prepares for day of protest a week after nationwide riots

sources.body: France is bracing for another weekend of protests, after violence erupted on the sidelines of last week's mobilisations. Paris is extending a partial curfew in parts of the city until Monday, while protests are banned altogether in the cities of Marseille and Lyon. 70,000 security personnel will be deployed on Saturday and only union demonstrations will be authorised.
sources.headline: French authorities tighten restrictions and ban specific protests

stories.headline: France investigates deadly shooting near Paris as a suspected racist terrorist attack

sources.body:
French President Emmanuel Macron has labelled a gun attack in a Parisian suburb which killed one person and injured five others "a racist terrorist attack".

Macron said the attack was a "turning point in the life of our Republic and our nation" - the first time there has ever been a random racial killing like this.

The attack unfolded over some 15 minutes with the attacker opening fire from his car - first in Trappes to the south-west of Paris, and then in nearby La Verrière - appearing to target people of migrant origin. He was subsequently arrested.

Three of those injured, including a 12-year-old girl, remain in a serious condition.

Visiting the scene of the attack in Trappes, Macron said people had been targeted for their skin colour or religion and urged the public not to give an inch in the face of what he called "ideologies taking root".

The exact motive remains unclear, but the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) said the incident appeared to be "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise".

The suspect has been named in French media as Kevin T who, according to PNAT, had four previous convictions which had been "automatically expunged".

The 39-year-old was known to police but not to France's intelligence services, local media report.

He was not on a list of individuals considered to be a serious threat to French security, the national anti-terrorism prosecutor's office told BFMTV.

A member of the suspect's "immediate family circle" was also taken into custody on Friday, it added.

The Mayor of Trappes, Ali Rabeh, said that "an individual fired shots from his vehicle at several people he encountered" on Friday morning.

The gunman drove through several neighbourhoods in a grey Renault Clio, according to witnesses. Rabeh said he had "fired randomly" with the seeming intent of causing "as many casualties as possible... he wanted to cause carnage", he said.

The mayor said people had been targeted at a petrol station, a medical centre and a playground in Trappes before the attacker had driven on to nearby La Verrière.

A police union official said the suspect had been detained in La Verrière on the main N10 road that runs through the town.

The mother of the injured 12-year-old told French broadcaster RTL her daughter suffered eight gunshot wounds and needed surgery.

"How could anyone do this to a child?" she asked.

The mother said her daughter had been wearing a headscarf and questioned whether this was why she was attacked.

"She's a child who was born in France, in Trappes. She has the right to live in France, to make her life in France," she added.

The attacker reportedly travelled down a main road, shooting intermittently out of his car window.

A local police chief told BFMTV that the suspect had used "an older-style semi-automatic weapon" with bursts of fire. Le Parisien reports that the gun dated back to World War Two.

PNAT said its investigation also includes "possession of a Category A weapon" - which includes military-grade weapons or weapons capable of firing in bursts.
sources.headline: Deadly shooting near Paris is a 'racist terrorist attack', Macron says

sources.body:
Gunman opens fire from car in Trappes and Verrière, killing one and injuring five others, including a 12-year-old girl

Emmanuel Macron has condemned racism in French society after a gunman opened fire from a car west of Paris on Friday, killing one person, wounding a 12-year-old girl and injuring four others in what the president called a “racist terrorist attack”.

Macron arrived at the scene of the drive-by shooting in Trappes on Friday night, saying he was deeply saddened by what he called the “premeditated” attack. The 12-year-old girl, who was shot eight times, is being treated in hospital.

“What happened today ​marks a turning point for our ⁠country; what happened today ​was ​a terrorist ​and racist attack,” ​Macron said.

He said the gunman had targeted people because of the colour of their skin. The president said racism had often become part of the “ambient discourse in France” and created “an atmosphere”.

He said: “Don’t let this terrorist attack divide us.” He called for “respect and unity”, saying many French people would be scared and thinking “this could happen to me”.

Ali Rabeh, the leftwing mayor of Trappes, said the gunman had set out by car on Friday morning “firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath” as he drove through the town and neighbouring La Verrière. The mayor called it “objectively a racist attack, probably Islamophobic”.

Rabeh, whose family has Moroccan roots, said: “The people targeted today could just as easily have been my mother, my brothers or my sisters-in-law.

“A 12-year-old girl is between life and death after being targeted by a volley of automatic gunfire in our country. Her crime was probably being of colour,” he added. “It’s probably one of the first attempts at a mass crime of Islamophobia and racism.”

Rabeh said everyone in France had a responsibility to bring “calm and harmony”. He called for a collective condemnation of rhetoric that “ideologically arms those capable of carrying out such acts”.

Anti-terrorism prosecutors are investigating whether the gunman targeted the “real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion” of the victims.

The 39-year-old suspect, who was stopped by police in his car, was named by France’s anti-terrorism prosecutor as Kevin T. He had driven through the towns of Trappes and La Verrière in Yvelines at about 10.30am on Friday. Over the course of 15 minutes, he repeatedly fired an automatic weapon, first at a petrol station, then a medical centre and a children’s playground.

The French public broadcaster reported that he shot dead a young black man, then targeted a woman wearing a headscarf, before shooting the 12-year-old girl, who was being treated for her eight gunshot wounds at a children’s hospital on Friday night.

The prosecutor said in a statement on Friday night that the medical status of the five wounded victims was not stable.

The man killed was named as Pengo Bossio Wangi in an Instagram post by the mixed martial arts academy of which he was a member. The Atch Academy paid tribute to a man who “set an example” and said that memories of “his smile, his energy, and his generosity will remain etched within our walls and in our hearts”.
sources.headline: Macron condemns racism after one killed in ‘terrorist’ shooting near Paris

sources.body: A gunman firing from a vehicle in a Paris suburb Friday killed one person and wounded several others, including a 12-year-old girl, in what French authorities suspect may have been a racially motivated attack.
sources.headline: Suspect arrested after 1 killed and 4 wounded in a shooting in Paris suburb

stories.headline: Seven people killed and dozens wounded in gun attack at a church funeral in Jordan

sources.body:
Seven people have been killed in an attack on a funeral in central Jordan, officials have said.

At least 34 others were injured as gunmen opened fire on a church in Hmoud, in the Karak governorate on Friday.

The unidentified gunmen are reported to have arrived in a car, entered the church and opened fire before fleeing. No-one has admitted carrying out the attack.

In a news conference, Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said authorities were working to apprehend the perpetrators which he described as a "group of extremists".

Jordan's King Abdullah II said authorities would "confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties".

Initial reports indicated seven people had been killed in the attack. A government spokesperson later said six people had died, before officials again revised the death toll to seven.

CCTV footage, verified by the BBC, appears to shows three gunmen making their way from a road toward the church.

Two of the attackers are seen making their way on to what appears to be a vehicle entrance to the church grounds, before retreating briefly and returning with a third man. All three appear to be armed with handguns.

Separate footage believed to be from the aftermath of the attack appears to show several dead and wounded bodies on the ground amid chaotic scenes.

Witnesses have described scenes of panic inside the church as people threw themselves under pews searching for cover, moving away from the windows.

Prayers and screams could be heard throughout the building as some tried to flee.

Khalid al-Mdanat was at the church and told BBC Arabic the attack lasted around 15 minutes with "people trying to flee while the shooting was still active".

"People began pushing and throwing themselves to the ground," he said.

"Some were taking cover, some were cradling the dead, others were holding their sons close, some were grabbing their children and fleeing, while others were holding onto their friends who were with them at the church."

He said the gunmen left through the church doors and fled in a pickup truck "firing as they went".

Another witness said: "I heard something as if a war had just started.

"I thought it was an electrical short circuit. I looked, people lying on the ground, wounded. The scene was catastrophic."

A woman in the church said explosions rang out seconds after a prayer.

"The sound of machine guns started, and the sound of glass. We began to realise that something was happening.

The witness described how the situation "continued to escalate for 10 continuous minutes". Once she ran out the church she said "bodies were all in the courtyards".

Al-Faraya has described the incident as "painful and horrific" and "unparalleled in the history of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan".

There was a heavy security presence at the entrance to a hospital treating people injured in the incident in Karak, amid an atmosphere charged with anger among residents of the governorate, particularly the families of those injured and killed.

Many looked distressed as roads were closed around the facility and people were forced to park their cars and continue on foot.
sources.headline: Seven shot dead by gunmen at church funeral in Jordan, officials say

sources.body:
Footage broadcast on state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.

The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 180km (110 miles) south of the capital, Amman.

Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen who appear to be holding pistols approaching the church and firing shots. A third man who appears to be holding a semiautomatic rifle then approaches and opens fire, and all three then run toward the church.

Video footage taken by witnesses shows broken glass and pools of blood on the floor of the church.

Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted 15 minutes after the funeral had started, and then people started running. “It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire,” Halasa said.

He did not see the gunmen, but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan’s security services did not immediately release details.

A government statement said that the attack was “carried out by unknown assailants,” but didn’t say whether any gunmen were captured or killed. It said that “investigations are under way at full speed”.

Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom’s Petra news agency.

Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff.

Jordan’s health minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of those wounded are in critical condition.

King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan “will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties” and offered his “deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded”.

Jordan’s prime minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was a result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants will be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism.

Condemnation of the slayings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman.

Ahmed al-Tayeb in Cairo, the grand imam of Al-Azhar, the Sunni Muslim world’s foremost religious institution, offered his condolences to the families of victims in Friday’s shooting, calling it a “heinous terrorist attack.”

Iraqi foreign minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and “affirmed Iraq’s solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism”, Hussein’s office said in a statement.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as “especially heinous,” spokesperson Stephane Dujarric said. “The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account.”
sources.headline: Seven killed and 40 injured after gunmen open fire at church funeral in Jordan

sources.body: At least seven people have been killed and 34 others wounded in a church shooting in Jordan, authorities said Friday. The unidentified assailants allegedly attacked the Greek Orthodox church during a funeral in the Karak directorate in the central part of the country.
sources.headline: Several killed, dozens wounded in Jordan church shooting

stories.headline: Israel begins Hebron demolitions and raids after two soldiers are killed

sources.body:
The Israeli military has begun demolishing Palestinian buildings in the city of Hebron, after two Israeli soldiers were killed in an attack by two Palestinian gunmen.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the military would "destroy" the neighbourhood where the two attackers came from, and that Israel was ready for "extensive action" in the occupied West Bank.

Three other soldiers were wounded in the attack at a checkpoint outside Hebron, before the gunmen were shot dead, officials say.

It comes at a time of high tensions, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days' time.

Footage verified by the BBC shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen. Other footage shows two gunmen exit a car armed with what appears to be a handgun and an assault rifle and start firing on soldiers at the checkpoint, before coming under return fire.

The incident has already begun to influence the ongoing election campaign, with Netanyahu - who has built his campaign on the promise of security - saying that his Likud party would cancel campaign events which had been set for Friday morning.

Speaking later from the scene, Netanyahu said that the military would "demolish this place and completely transform it," referring to the Hebron neighbourhood where the attackers are said to have come from.

It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.

Netanyahu likened his plans to previous operations in West Bank refugee camps where residential buildings were demolished and thousands were displaced.

He also said he had reviewed plans for the largest military operation in the West Bank in decades - though did not say when it could be carried out.

He added that he had imposed cordons around the city of Hebron - which has around 200,000 residents - and the nearby city of Halhul.

Netanyahu's far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for Israel to launch a campaign in the West Bank "exactly like in Gaza or Lebanon," while far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir called for Israel to dismantle the Palestinian Authority.

On Thursday, Foreign Minister Israel Katz accused opposition leaders of undermining the government by criticising Netanyahu's warnings of an attack ahead of the election, saying they would be "responsible" for any future attack on the country.

Opposition chiefs, including frontrunner Gadi Eisenkot and former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, offered their condolences to the families of the killed troops and praised those who killed the attackers.

The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle, and that they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there.
sources.headline: Israeli forces begin demolishing Palestinian buildings in Hebron after two Israeli soldiers shot dead

sources.body:
Benjamin Netanyahu and ministers promise demolitions and forced displacement after deadly gunfight

Israel has launched a campaign of collective punishment against Palestinians in Hebron after gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers and injured three near a checkpoint outside the city.

Benjamin Netanyahu announced a siege on Hebron and neighbouring Halhul and said residents of the gunmen’s home neighbourhoods would all be forced out. He promised mass demolitions of homes.

The first destruction began within hours of the attack, as ministers who had been on the campaign trail ahead of elections on Tuesday rushed to the site of the shooting.

The far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, posted a video of himself in front of a bulldozer as it tore down a Palestinian home near the site of the firefight.

The destruction of a home built without permits aimed to “create deterrence and exact a price”, Smotrich said. There was no claim of a connection between the building’s owners and the attackers.

Soon after the destruction began, Israel’s high court issued a temporary order to stop the demolitions. A human rights lawyer, Mohammed Dahleh, filed an urgent petition on behalf of two factory owners nearby, arguing that the demolition violated international law on collective punishment and Israeli administrative law.

“What we saw today was an attempt to copy the illegal practices used in Gaza, in the heart of the West Bank ,” Dahleh said. “They want to wipe out entire areas exactly as they did in Gaza and the refugee camps in the West Bank.”

Michael Sfard, a leading Israeli lawyer, said Smotrich’s video was a “direct admission” that the demolitions were a collective punishment. He noted that deterrence had been used as an excuse for collective punishment since antiquity.

The defence minister, Israel Katz, promised further mass demolitions and forced displacement. He drew an explicit comparison with Gaza and said Hebron would be targeted in the same way as Jenin refugee camp, where nearly 20,000 people have been forced from their homes. Hebron is the largest Palestinian city in the occupied West Bank, with about 250,000 residents.

Katz said: “The Jenin refugee camp model arrives in Hebron. Every clan neighbourhood in Hebron from which the terrorists emerged today will be evacuated of its residents. Just like in Gaza, just like in Lebanon.”

Netanyahu announced that plans had been drawn up for the largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967, when Israeli forces occupied the Palestinian territory and forcibly displaced about 300,000 Palestinians.

No date had been set “but it is on the way”, he said in a statement that also pledged mass forced displacement and demolitions in Hebron and the expansion of Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

The attack was launched by two men armed with an assault rifle and a handgun, according to the Israeli military. The men, who were driving a car with Israeli number plates, opened fire after they were stopped by soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron. They were killed after a 20-minute gunfight.
sources.headline: Israel launches collective punishment campaign in Hebron after two soldiers killed

sources.body:
Israeli military raid targets at least 15 towns in the northern West Bank, including Nablus and Jenin.

Israel imposes full closure of occupied West Bank after Hebron shooting kills two soldiers

Israeli forces have raided towns, detaining dozens of Palestinians, hours after Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced ordering a full lockdown of the occupied West Bank following an attack in the city of Hebron that killed two Israeli soldiers.

Israeli forces raided at least 15 towns in the northern West Bank, detaining dozens of Palestinians, Al Jazeera correspondents reported on Saturday.

The military raids targeted several northern cities and towns, including Nablus, Jenin, Tubas and Qalqilya.

In Nablus, Israeli forces carried out arrests and raided Palestinian homes in the villages of Jalud and Qaryut. Arrests were also reported in Arrabeh and Burqin, near Jenin, while Israeli forces entered Tubas and the nearby town of Aqqaba.

In the southern occupied West Bank, Israeli bulldozers demolished a three-storey building in Hebron, with families given five minutes to collect their belongings. Israeli forces also ordered hundreds of Palestinian families to forcibly evacuate their homes in the Ein Deir Bahha area of Hebron and its surroundings.

Israeli troops also surrounded the home of one of the suspects in the shooting attack that killed two Israeli soldiers in Hebron, while carrying out raids in the city’s al-Jalda neighbourhood.

The Israeli army said late on Friday that its forces began an operation in Hebron that would last “for several days”, in addition to operations by other forces in “dozens” of areas across the West Bank.

Further east, Israeli forces entered Jericho and the nearby Aqabat Jabr refugee camp.

With the lockdown, nearly 1,000 checkpoints and gates across the West Bank will be closed, affecting millions of Palestinians.

Netanyahu gave the order on Friday, shortly after the Israeli military said it had killed two Palestinian gunmen who attacked a reserve battalion near the Israeli settlement of Telem, killing two soldiers.

Israel’s ambulance service reported that at least three Israeli soldiers were injured in addition to the two who died.

All Israeli settlements, including Telem, are illegal under international law.

The attack and clampdown came amid heightened tensions across the Palestinian territory as Israeli settlers and soldiers engage in violent pogroms . Attacks on olive harvesters have been rife as aggression has been on the rise before the coming Israeli elections on Tuesday.

Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir responded to the killing of the Israeli soldiers by calling for Israel to take full control of the West Bank, in which the Israeli government is encouraging the construction of numerous settlements.

Mustafa Barghouti, secretary-general of the Palestinian National Initiative political party, said incitement from far-right Israeli ministers is making the situation worse.

The closure turns every city and village into “a small prison”, with checkpoints and gates blocking healthcare, the economy and education, he told Al Jazeera. He warned that collective punishment “will lead to explosions”.
sources.headline: Israel raids towns, detains dozens of Palestinians in occupied West Bank

stories.headline: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures hundreds in Taiwan as it moves toward China

sources.body:
Super typhoon weakening but large parts of Taiwan, including Taipei, still mostly closed and flights cancelled

Typhoon Champi swept past Taiwan on Saturday killing one person, injuring more than 500, and uprooting trees and severing power as it weakened and ⁠headed north toward ⁠the ​Chinese coast.

Earlier classified as a super typhoon and one of the strongest storms in the ⁠Pacific this year, Champi was still packing gusts of about 126km per hour (78 miles per hour) near its ⁠centre, according to Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA).

The storm was about ​150km (93 miles) east ‌of Taiwan, the CWA ‌said, having glanced off the island’s northeast coast in the early ‌hours of Saturday.

Champi’s forecast track shows it turning north toward the Chinese coast before eventually moving into southern Japan .

Taiwan’s fire department said one man had been killed, swept by waves from the ‌island of Liuqiu. Another 527 people were injured during heavy wind and torrential rain.

Taipower said more than 167,000 homes had lost electricity, but most had now been reconnected.

Large parts of northern and central Taiwan, including Taipei, declared a second ​day of ‌office and ​school closures ​on Saturday, and some flights were still being cancelled.

Taiwan is generally well prepared for typhoons, which keeps casualties low. Although more common in summer, the storms can strike also in autumn.
sources.headline: Typhoon Champi kills one and injures more than 500 in Taiwan as it heads to China

sources.body:
Authorities warn of ‘destructive winds’ and urge residents to shelter as the storm passes the island’s northeast.

Typhoon Champi has struck Taiwan, killing one person and injuring more than 500 others, as authorities warned of “destructive winds” and instructed people to stay indoors.

The storm swept past the island’s northeast on Friday, toppling trees, triggering brief flooding, disrupting power lines and forcing more than 5,000 people to evacuate from their homes.

Emergency crews were sent on Saturday to restore power to about 56,000 households still without electricity, authorities said. Most shops in northern and central Taiwan stayed shut for a second day as the storm edged away from the northeast and headed north.

Champi is heading towards China and Japan, forcing flight cancellations in the region.

Taiwan’s Ministry of Transportation and Communications said 259 flights were cancelled, an improvement from Friday, when the number was almost 1,000.

Champi was briefly a super typhoon with winds of nearly 300 kilometres per hour (186 miles per hour) but has since weakened. The US Joint Typhoon Warning Center on Friday reported maximum winds of 185km/h (115mph).

Worse is still expected to come on Saturday. Champi could drop up to 900mm (35 inches) of rain between Thursday and Saturday, with the northeast hit hardest, Taiwan’s Central Weather Administration (CWA) said. More than 400mm fell in Yilan County on Friday.

The forecaster also said the storm weakened overnight as it looped off the city of Yilan, which has received 650mm of rain since Thursday.

CWA forecaster Lu Kuo-chen said the typhoon could slow near the island’s northeastern tip, prolonging its impact.

“It was most terrifying around midnight,” a retired teacher surnamed Lin told the Reuters news agency as he inspected downed banana trees in his garden in Yilan. “It was a sleepless night. I haven’t seen anything like this in many years.”

Taipei resident Thomas Wang, 70, said the storm felt like something out of the horror film “Poltergeist”.

Martha Wang, a 55-year-old secretary, told the AFP news agency that she feared being “blown away” as her scooter shook on a bridge in New Taipei City.

While William Yu, a 55-year-old librarian, told AFP that the storm “wasn’t any stronger than other typhoons”.

About 8,400 households in Japan’s Okinawa islands were without power on Friday afternoon, according to the Okinawa Electric Power Company. The government said two people were injured in the typhoon in Japan’s southernmost prefecture.

Champi is forecast to hover near Okinawa and then China’s eastern coast before turning northeast, towards mainland Japan.

Chinese authorities warned of “strong winds and heavy rain” as the typhoon approaches mainland China’s east coast, the state-run broadcaster reported. It said parts of Jiangsu, Shanghai and Zhejiang could see heavy to torrential rain.

Some train services were suspended and tens of thousands of people evacuated in Shanghai.

Champi is the latest storm in a Pacific season supercharged by El Nino.
sources.headline: Typhoon Champi hits Taiwan, killing one and injuring hundreds

stories.headline: Kenya records a second Ebola death as concern grows over the outbreak’s spread

sources.body:
Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.

A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.

Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.

All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.

More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.

Kenya's latest victim was a "direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms" on 13 October, the health ministry said.

The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.

Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.

The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.

Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.

The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.

The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.

Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.

Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.

Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.

Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.

It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.

In another development, Nigeria's health minister has said the country's single confirmed case of Ebola appears to be genetically related to a strain identified earlier in Kenya.
sources.headline: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya

sources.body: In tonight's programme, scramble to get through rubble to trapped survivors after a more than 10 storeys building being built in Nairobi goes down. Also, Kenya says that there's been a second Ebola death. Earlier this week it had logged 9 cases so far, all traced back to its first Ebola patient who died earlier this month. And in finally the 11th edition of the iconic contemporary art festival Also known as Africa taking place in Paris, we speak to Cape Verde's artist Amadeo Carvalho.
sources.headline: Building collapse in Nairobi search for survivors under way

stories.headline: House battlegrounds tighten as Republicans spend heavily to defend vulnerable seats

sources.body: Senior Democrats are tempering their expectations about how big of a House majority they might win, as both parties see a tightening battlefield. The latest rounds of internal polling from both parties from the middle of October show GOP candidates gaining ground in the Midwest and narrowing races in a key Colorado seat and elsewhere, according to six people familiar with the data who were granted anonymity to discuss it. Republicans’ deluge of money also seems to be helping shore up some imperiled Florida seats even as they face serious problems in North Carolina and Texas. The GOP gerrymandered those three states in their favor in the Trump-induced round of redistricting following the 2024 election. Now, Democrats on Capitol Hill are starting to privately caution some of their bolder colleagues that it seems very possible they don’t hit the 235-seat height of their majority following the 2018 elections, according to one of those people and two others with direct knowledge of the conversations. “I don’t think anyone ever believed we were going to have 2018 numbers,” one House Democrat said. “I honestly think the results are going to be all over the place. Caution seems smart to me. But, optimistic is also a good place to be.” That’s a notable change from the tune some Democrats were singing just earlier this month: Brooke Butler, political director for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, had predicted that their majority this cycle could reach 240 seats. “Anywhere between 218 and 240 feels very viable,” she told POLITICO earlier this month in announcing the DCCC’s plans to target new districts deep in GOP territory. Some Democrats feel their own internal polling is over-indexing their strength in some cases, according to two other operatives working on competitive races, granted anonymity to speak candidly. But the party is still confident they’ll win the majority and are eager to keep Republicans spending to defend once-safe red seats. Before the all-out GOP panic started in late September and boosted many Democrats’ bullishness, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries predicted House Democrats would win 220 seats. “Given the mountain of outside, billionaire-backed cash being dropped in competitive House races across the country and the seemingly never-ending schemes by Republicans to try to rig the midterms — we’ve always known that the majority-making races would come down to the wire,” DCCC spokesperson Viet Shelton said in a statement. “We’re clear-eyed that House Democrats are poised to win the majority, and it will take running flat out until Election Day.” Still, the tightening in the core House battleground districts that were identified as battlegrounds early on means a slew of those races are currently within the margin of error, or Republicans in some cases are running just a few points behind, according to the six people with knowledge of the internal Democratic and GOP polling. That includes the race for Michigan’s 7th District between GOP Rep. Tom Barrett and Democrat William Lawrence. Another marquee battleground in Wisconsin’s 3rd District has tightened a few points since last month, as Republicans pour in millions of dollars more in ad spending. Democrat Rebecca Cooke is running 1 percentage point ahead of GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in a multi-candidate vote, 47% to 46%, according to an internal Cooke campaign poll from mid-October obtained by POLITICO. "Wisconsin is always close and hard-fought — especially in a district Trump won decisively,” a Cooke campaign aide said. “Our working class message is connecting, but we need the resources to make sure it's heard." In Iowa, Republicans still feel they’re likely to lose Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks 1st District. But they’re cautiously optimistic about Rep. Zach Nunn in Iowa’s 3rd district and Joe Mitchell in Iowa’s open 2nd District, where President Donald Trump is set to hold a rally on Nov. 1. “Any Republican in Iowa in a neck and neck race ends up winning on Election Day,” said one GOP operative working on House races, who was granted anonymity to discuss the landscape. Top GOP staff and officials still believe it’s more likely than not that they lose the House majority, but they’re hopeful they can limit Democrats’ margin. The new polling is helping them see they might avoid some of the deep hemorrhaging, especially in the Midwest, that they feared in late September and earlier this month. That region has been hit hardest by Trump’s tariff agenda and rising diesel costs resulting from an unpopular Iran war — something the White House has seemed to acknowledge, with Trump promising $8 billion to farmers hurting from high fuel prices. “Democrats spent months measuring the drapes, and now they’re scrambling to lower expectations before a single race is called,” National Republican Congressional Committee spokesperson Mike Marinella said. “Republicans have been laser-focused since day one and built our operation to win the races that will get us to 218.” Trump is also personally working to shore up at-risk Republicans in his home state of Florida with a visit Friday to rally GOP voters. Republicans in the last few days started to pile money into a series of once-safe GOP seats there, including Rep. Anna Paulina Luna’s Gulf Coast seat. Republicans are also racing to save several open seats, despite redrawing the districts in their favor, where the GOP is struggling. House Majority Leader Steve Scalise is in South Florida to boost GOP Rep. Maria Salazar on Friday and campaigned on Thursday for Republican Dan Green in the redrawn seat against Rep. Darren Soto, who should be toast under the GOP gerrymander in most political environments. Senior Republicans believe the money bomb is starting to help shore up some Florida seats, though they still have more work to do. South Texas remains one of the worst spots on the map for House Republicans, after the top House GOP super PAC cut off spending for one of their star recruits — Tano Tijerina, who is challenging Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar — to help other imperiled GOP candidates. Some at-risk Republicans in the area, like Rep. Monica De La Cruz, should’ve been safe in a recently redrawn seat. In North Carolina, Republicans are facing some dire fallout across House seats after the implosion of Republican Michael Whatley’s Senate campaign and top Senate GOP groups cutting off spending in the state. Top House GOP groups and Trump’s political operation have already cut off spending in North Carolina’s open 11th District, where Democrat Jamie Ager is challenging Republican Jennifer Balkcom.

stories.headline: Poll finds Trump is motivating more Democratic opposition voters than Republican supporters ahead of the midterms

sources.body: President Donald Trump is asking voters to “pretend” he is on the ballot. That might backfire. New results from The POLITICO Poll show that Democratic midterm voters are more motivated to oppose the president than Republican voters are to support him. Many Republican voters also aren’t looking for blind loyalty to Trump in the midterms: Half say they’d rather their local candidate aim to win, even if it means speaking out against the president. It’s not uncommon for voters in the party out of power to be more motivated in a midterm year. But the lopsided findings are an ominous sign for Trump, who has fundamentally reshaped the GOP over the past decade and has once again staked his brand — and political capital — on delivering wins for Republicans in November. With less than two weeks before the election, the poll suggests Republicans are pragmatic, and care more about preventing a blue wave than standing by Trump. And in a year when voter frustration over high prices appears poised to play a major role, that distinction could prove consequential. The poll, conducted by London-based firm PF Global, reveals the extent to which frustration with Trump is driving Democrats: Nearly half of Democratic midterm voters say they will be voting “mainly to oppose President Trump,” compared to just 38% of Republican voters who say they will be voting mainly to show support for Trump. Instead, a plurality of Republican midterm voters — 48% — say their main motivation when casting a vote is to show support for a local candidate. Only 37% of Democratic voters agree. “[Trump is] 100% motivating Democrats more than Republicans,” said Doug Heye, a longtime GOP strategist. “That may have been the case regardless, but it’s even more true with words like ‘diesel’ and ‘Iran ’ now a part of everyday political discussion.” Half of Republicans think candidates have a better chance of winning if they align themselves with Trump rather than breaking from him, compared to just 30% who believe candidates would have a better chance of winning if they break away. But half of Republicans also accept their candidates speaking out against the president if that’s what they need to do to win their own election. That’s compared with 37% who say candidates should remain loyal to the president and support his agenda, even if it means risking a loss. On top of that, majorities of Republican voters say Trump himself should give candidates some room to break with him on specific policy issues to win elections. If it helps GOP candidates’ chances of winning, they said, the president should allow for disagreement on the speed of AI development, the cost of living, and whether the war in Iran was a good decision. That holds true for pluralities or even majorities of Trump 2024 voters who self-identify as part of the “MAGA” movement across each policy area, suggesting that even his most loyal voters want the president to let candidates distance themselves if it can help them win. “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress,” said White House spokesperson Davis Ingle. RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre said "POLITICO didn't need to conduct a poll to know that Democrats are motivated by their hatred for President Trump and Republicans.” She added that the GOP is "running on actual accomplishments like cutting taxes and securing the border," while saying Democrats have made "investigations, obstruction, and impeachment" their campaign platform. Still, the tension is playing out in real time as Republican candidates locked in competitive races walk a tightrope between maintaining Trump’s support — and that of his MAGA base — without alienating critical moderate and independent voters. They’re especially under pressure as Trump hits the campaign trail in battlegrounds and red states, with several candidates having to quietly make calculations whether it will hurt them politically to appear next to him. “I think Republicans ... are stuck choosing which finger to cut off,” said a national GOP operative, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the midterm landscape. "There is no good answer." In Iowa, where voter frustration over some of Trump’s marquee policies, including tariffs and rising costs stemming from the Iran war, has mounted, Republican candidates have sought to create some distance from the president. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, the party’s Senate nominee, has said the war needs to be “ brought to a successful and immediate end .” She also skipped a rally Vice President JD Vance held in the state last month. Several other GOP candidates have also skipped Trump rallies in their home states, and many have grown increasingly wary of mentioning Trump in ads , including in red states that over the last few months have suddenly started to look competitive. In battleground Georgia, GOP gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson has carefully navigated his relationship with Trump, avoiding public breaks with the president on policy but still limiting direct references to him in campaign ads and on the debate stage. “I don’t know that Trump coming [to Georgia] helps Republicans more so than it excites Democrats, especially in a wave election year,” said Jason Shepherd, a former Cobb County GOP chair who is supporting Jackson. That leaves Republican candidates in a tricky position: Their voters are willing to accept breaking from Trump if victory is on the line, but voters — and candidates — won’t know what will cost them their race until it's too late. "There's no reason to gratuitously attack the White House and make an enemy,” the national GOP operative said. “But the end game here is to get reelected, and if they have to get reelected, but the president's annoyed at them for a period of time, they'll get over it.” While Republican candidates balance loyalty to Trump with the possibility of breaking away on certain issues, Democratic midterm voters remain highly motivated to vote against Trump’s agenda. Even Trump’s endorsement of a Republican candidate seems to influence Democrats more than Republicans: Roughly 70% of Democratic midterm voters say his endorsement would make them less likely to support a candidate, compared to 55% of Republican midterm voters who say the endorsement would make them more likely to support a candidate. “The midterm elections are about anger management and failed expectations,” said North Carolina based GOP strategist Paul Shumaker. “A lot of Republicans and swing voters feel like their expectations have not been met in helping address their economic concerns.” Alec Hernández and Alisa Vasquez contributed to this story.
sources.headline: Poll: Trump is mobilizing more Democrats against him than Republicans for him

stories.headline: New York ambulance delays fuel proposal for real-time updates to emergency callers

sources.body: 911 EMERGENCY: An ambulance in New York City now takes an average of 13 minutes to reach someone in life-threatening distress. That response time has risen five years straight and is up 41.2% from a decade ago, a city comptroller’s report revealed earlier this month . According to this year’s Mayor’s Management Report, which came out in September, ambulance response times to life-threatening emergencies shot up by almost 16% between fiscal year 2025 and fiscal year 2026 — the sharpest increase this decade. A core part of the issue is that calling 911 does not necessarily mean an ambulance will be immediately dispatched. Callers are put in dispatch queues. If a higher-priority call comes through, the ambulance might be rerouted. And all of this happens behind the scenes — which means those experiencing medical emergencies have no idea when help will actually arrive. Council member Joann Ariola, chair of the Fire and Emergency Management Committee, proposed a bill in August that would require the city to send New Yorkers broad notifications when the emergency response system is overloaded. Now, the Queens Republican is pushing for these notifications to be completely personalized. “The idea is that I would be able to track my ambulance in real time, just like you’re able to do for your bus, or your train, or your rideshare car,” she told Playbook. If patients know how far away help is, they can make an informed decision to forgo an ambulance and instead pursue other means of transportation to a hospital, she said. That would also alleviate pressure on the already overloaded EMS system and potentially get callers the care they need faster. The idea has support from a council member across the political aisle. “We get live texts about everything under the sun, but for some reason, in our current system, we don’t get alerts about this,” Democratic Council member Harvey Epstein said. “If I’m waiting for an ambulance because my kid broke their leg, and I learn that it’s going to be half an hour, it’s smarter for me to just hop in a cab anyway.” Ariola said she met with top FDNY officials — including Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore, Chief of Department John Esposito and Chief of EMS Paul Miano — ahead of Tuesday’s hearing to discuss the idea. All of them, she said, appeared more receptive to specific text alerts than to the broad notification system proposed in her initial bill. Amanda Farinacci, an FDNY spokesperson, said the department is “considering and exploring all options that will help us respond to emergency medical calls quickly and keep New Yorkers informed.” "We are exploring all our options, this included,” she said, referring to the live text-update model. Ariola said she’s submitted the new version of the bill and is waiting to hear back from the legislative affairs committee. The solution proposed by she and Epstein would address the public-facing side of the problem, offering relief to callers in emergency situations. The root cause of the issue, though, is retaining EMS employees — a challenge officials and union leaders say stems from low pay for a high-stress job. “This is not fixing the broken system,” Ariola said. “We are in a state of emergency right now. It’s a systemic problem with EMS because they cannot retain their members, because it’s not a career.” Entry-level pay for emergency medical technicians is less than that of sanitation workers, firefighters, correction officers and police officers. Since 2019, about 4,300 EMTs and paramedics have left their titles, many for better-paying jobs elsewhere in the department. Last fiscal year, 58% of departing EMTs became firefighters. The union representing emergency medical workers is negotiating a contract that lapsed in 2022, and it’s seeking pay parity with firefighters. But the comptroller’s report found that parity alone would raise EMS salary-related expenses by $184 million a year, a 66% jump. “The City can reverse this dangerous trend by ensuring members of EMS are treated as equals to members of fire operations, and by providing EMS personnel with pay and benefit parity comparable to their firefighter counterparts,” Local 3621 President Vincent Variale and Local 2507 President Michael Greco said in a joint statement. “These actions would not only treat our EMS workforce respectfully and properly; they would save the lives of New Yorkers in peril.” Response times to life-threatening emergencies saw the sharpest year-to-year increase of the decade between the last two fiscal years, a timeframe that straddles the Mamdani administration and the administration of former Mayor Eric Adams. “This is something that each mayor inherited, but the new administration, it is now absolutely their issue,” Ariola said. “I’m hoping this is the administration that finally solves the retention problem. And the only way to solve that problem is to pay EMTs their worth and also recognize them as uniformed workers.” The mayor’s office declined to comment on Ariola’s new proposal and referred to a comment from the fire department. “The Department is currently engaged in a challenging period of increasing response times. We know this is unacceptable and we are working tirelessly to reverse this trend,” Farinacci said. “We will continue to take steps to improve response times and keep New Yorkers safe, including improving coordination with hospitals, enhancing efficiency in high-volume areas, and increased operational visibility to help return units to service quickly."  — Molly Reinmann FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL A SUBURBAN ALARM: Suburban voters across the country are turning against President Donald Trump, according to a poll that amounts to a major warning sign for the GOP this election season. The results of the National Suburban Poll by the National Center for Suburban Studies at Hofstra University paint a bleak picture for Trump and his party. “Numbers that are concerning Republicans throughout the country become even more so when they show up in suburbs, which for years have been the ‘swing’ voting bloc that determines national and many statewide elections,” said Larry Levy, the center’s dean. “When a party’s or candidate’s numbers are weak in the suburbs, as we’ve found in many instances for Republicans, the situation goes from concerning to alarming.” The survey found 33% of suburban voters approve of the president’s job performance. His approval rating in swing suburban House seats isn’t much better: 35%. Just over a quarter of suburban voters nationally — 26% — are satisfied with the direction of the country. Suburban voters by a margin of 50% to 42% prefer Democrats over Republicans in the generic Congressional ballot question. The GOP, though, is in a statistical tie with Democrats in suburban swing seats. In those districts, Democrats lead Republicans 47% to 44%. Taken together, the numbers highlight the challenge Republicans face this year, especially in deep blue New York, home to several swing House districts in the New York City suburbs. The most competitive race is in the Hudson Valley, where GOP Rep. Mike Lawler is fending off a challenge from Democratic opponent Cait Conley. The survey included 1,500 people nationwide and was conducted in late September. It oversampled suburban residents who live in swing House districts. — Nick Reisman SARATOGA FRESH: To get an idea of how much national headwinds might apply to the New York State Senate, look to Saratoga County. Plenty of indicators suggest two factors will heavily influence the outcome: Voters are angry at Republicans and willing to oppose well-tenured incumbents. That could be a double-barreled problem for Sen. Jim Tedisco, who’s running in a district where Donald Trump lost by 8 points two years ago. The Republican is now the dean of the state Legislature by a large margin: Tedisco came to Albany in 1983, the first year of Mario Cuomo’s time as governor. Only four other members who might be in office next year served in 1999. “Jim Tedisco’s been in office for over 40 years, almost as long as I’ve been alive,” said Sarah Rogerson, Tedisco’s Democratic challenger. “People are ready for some fresh voices.” Even if current assumptions about the electorate’s mood prove true, Republicans remain optimistic they won’t apply to New York. The GOP believes 2026 will be a repeat of 2022, when a lack of enthusiasm for the top of the ticket meant a good year for Democrats nationwide bypassed the Empire State. “If there’s going to be a blue wave across the country, it’s probably going to miss New York, and it’s largely because of how deeply unpopular Kathy Hochul is,” Senate Republican Campaign Committee Chair George Borrello said. Nobody’s predicting Republicans will retake the majority in a chamber where Democrats had a 41-22 edge this year. The main question now is whether Democrats can pull off a two-thirds supermajority of 42 or more members, a feat accomplished in 2020 and 2022 but not 2024. READ MORE in POLITICO Pro from Bill Mahoney. FROM CITY HALL BILL SIGNING TIME: Mayor Zohran Mamdani will sign two bills passed by the City Council that come with significant transit and housing policy ramifications, his office confirmed today. The first measure Mamdani plans to put his John Hancock on will abolish New York City’s horse carriage industry . The second will give nonprofit groups and local land trusts first dibs on buying distressed residential properties in their communities, with the idea that those regulations will protect affordable housing stock. Mamdani had already voiced support for both pieces of legislation before the Council passed them yesterday. But his office hadn’t until today confirmed he would sign the bills, as opposed to letting them lapse into law. Mamdani’s office did not immediately provide a date for when he plans to sign the bills. The issue of signing bills came to the fore this week when the New York Post noted that Mamdani has only inked one bill since taking office. Ultimately, as long as the mayor doesn’t veto a bill, there’s no practical difference between whether he signs it or lets it lapse, as it becomes law regardless. — Chris Sommerfeldt  IN OTHER NEWS — IN THE SCHOOLS: New York City is considering closing a Harlem high school due to underenrollment, the first in what could be a growing number of school mergers and closures amid public school enrollment declines. ( Chalkbeat ) — HOCHUL: The governor’s vision for New York is largely shaped by her upbringing in a small Rust Belt city in western New York and her family’s slow climb up the socioeconomic ladder. ( New York Times ) — CORNELL 7: Attorney General Letitia James is asking a court to dismiss a request to remove her from the investigation into the alleged sexual assault at Cornell University due to impartiality concerns. ( Times Union ) Missed this morning’s New York Playbook? We forgive you. Read it here .

sources.headline: El Supremo exige al Gobierno la lista de los afectados por la ‘ley de nietos’ y amenaza de multa y posible responsabilidad penal si no lo hace

sources.body:
El Tribunal Supremo ha dado un plazo de cinco días , hasta el próximo 28 de octubre, a los ministros de Presidencia, Justicia y Relaciones con las Cortes, Félix Bolaños, y al ministro de Asuntos Exteriores, José Manuel Albares, para que remitan la relación "nominal" de las 163.020 personas afectadas por la suspensión cautelar del derecho a voto a los inscritos en el Centro de Residentes Ausentes (CERA) tras la aplicación de la llamada 'ley de nietos' , con apercibimiento de multa o deducción de testimonio.

En concreto, les advierte de que si el día 28 de octubre a las 15:00 horas no han enviado esa información, la Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo podrá acordar una "multa coercitiva" de 1.000 euros , o podría haber "otras responsabilidades patrimoniales" e incluso "deducir, en su caso, el oportuno testimonio de particulares para exigir la responsabilidad penal que pudiera corresponder".

En dos autos a los que ha tenido acceso RTVE, la Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo ordena que además de remitirle al Supremo la relación "nominal" de los afectados, que también envíen a la Oficina del Censo Electoral la documentación de "todas las personas inscritas en el CERA".

Además, reclama que se advierta de quienes hayan adquirido la nacionalidad por la llamada 'ley de nietos' que figuren en él a fecha 1 de agosto de 2026, se les comunique que lo están "con carácter provisional", pues solo podrán votar aquellas personas a los que los Registros Consulares les hayan expedido "certificación acreditativa de su condición de nacidos fuera de España" de exiliados españoles "por razones políticas, ideológicas o de creencia o de orientación de identidad sexual y que hubieran perdido o renunciado a la nacionalidad española".

La decisión del Supremo llega dos días después de que el Tribunal Constitucional haya rechazado admitir a trámite el recurso de amparo que presentó el Defensor del Pueblo, Ángel Gabilondo, contra la resolución del alto tribunal de suspender cautelarmente el derecho al voto a los nacionalizados por la 'ley de nietos', por considerlo "prematuro".

Según la Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo, "hasta el momento presente", solo se les ha facilitado esa cifra de 163.020 personas , "sin ningún dato adicional más", y que este miércoles recibieron "tres documentos que contienen dos informes informes de la Dirección General de Españoles en el Exterior y Asuntos Consulares y uno del Instituto Nacional de Estadística".

Además, la Sala apunta que, de acuerdo esos informes, solo " han sido revisados un total de 31.390 expedientes, de los que se han expedido un total de 91 certificados " de personas que "han acreditado el exilio de sus ascendientes en los términos que establecieron" los dos autos por los que acordó la suspensión cautelar.

Y advierte también ante la proximidad de las elecciones generales del 29 de noviembre, que por la "aplicación de las medidas cautelares de suspensión impuestas, estas personas pueden verse imposibilitadas finalmente del ejercicio de su derecho al voto por la propia inacción de la Administración ".

Sesión de control al Gobierno en el Congreso de los Diputados. / José Luis Roca

El Ministerio de Exteriores asegura que ha movilizado todos los recursos disponibles para cumplir la última de las órdenes del Tribunal Supremo. Va a poner a trabajar este fin de semana al personal de los consulados implicados en la elaboración de la lista de los afectados por la suspensión cautelar del voto ordenada por el Alto Tribunal.

La Sala de lo Contencioso-Administrativo del Tribunal Supremo ha dado un plazo de cinco días a los ministros de Justicia y Asuntos Exteriores, Félix Bolaños y José Manuel Albares, respectivamente, para que le remitan antes del próximo día 28 los nombres de las 163.020 personas nacionalizadas por la 'ley de nietos' afectadas por la suspensión cautelar de la inscripción en el censo electoral de residentes ausentes (CERA) acordada el pasado 10 de septiembre y ratificada el pasado día 12, informa Ángeles Vázquez. Hasta ahora, según señala el alto tribunal en su resolución, la Administración solo ha podido acreditar la condición de descendiente de exiliados en 91 de los más de 31.000 casos revisados .

Según fuentes del departamento dirigido por José Manuel Albares a este periódico, desde la recepción de los primeros autos "se suspendieron los permisos y vacaciones en los consulados" y se ordenó "destinar a esta tarea todo el personal necesario" , incluidos efectivos de las embajadas.

Exteriores afirma que ha autorizado "todas las solicitudes de refuerzo de plantilla" presentadas por las oficinas consulares y que ha dado instrucciones para que los funcionarios "trabajen en esta tarea este sábado y domingo, con el objetivo de cumplir el último auto" con el plazo fijado por el alto tribunal. "El Ministerio de Asuntos Exteriores y todos los consulados de España están realizando todos los esfuerzos necesarios desde el primer auto del Tribunal Supremo", señalan las mismas fuentes, que aseguran que "se van a redoblar esfuerzos si aún cabe para cumplir con este nuevo auto".

En sendos autos, uno por la demanda de Iustitia Europa y otro por la de Vox, la Sala Tercera, con el voto particular de la magistrada Alicia Millán, incluye la amenaza de la imposición de una "multa coercitiva por importe de 1.000 euros" a los ministros que incumplan su requerimiento , a la vez que les advierte de que se reiterarán las multas "hasta la completa ejecución del fallo judicial, sin perjuicio de otras responsabilidades patrimoniales a que hubiere lugar". Añade que si considera que su incumplimiento reviste caracteres de delito, actuará contra ellos.

El Alto Tribunal señala que " no aprecia obstáculo alguno" a que la Junta Electoral Central proceda a la remisión del primer envío de documentación electoral , prevista entre este sábado y el día 30. No obstante, le pide que incluya la advertencia de que "quienes hayan adquirido la nacionalidad española de origen por el derecho de opción previsto en la disposición adicional 8ª de la ley de memoria democrática, esto es los 'nacidos fuera de España de padre o madre, abuelo o abuela, que originariamente hubieran sido españoles, y que, como consecuencia de haber sufrido exilio por razones políticas, ideológicas o de creencia o de orientación e identidad sexual, hubieran perdido o renunciado a la nacionalidad española'" están inscritos en el CERA "con carácter provisional" .

stories.headline: Feijóo signals willingness to rely on Vox to form a parliamentary majority after Spain’s election

sources.body: <p>El presidente del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, se ha mostrado dispuesto este viernes a “completar” con Vox la mayoría parlamentaria que salga de las urnas el próximo 29 de noviembre. “Mi primer objetivo es que Sánchez se vaya del Gobierno”, ha afirmado Feijóo en una <a href="https://cadenaser.com/" target="_self" rel="" title="https://cadenaser.com/">entrevista en la Cadena SER</a>. Con esa prioridad, el líder popular ha aparcado la petición de que gobierne la lista más votada, lo que antes de los comicios de 2023 se había convertido en uno de los ejes de su campaña. Como carta de presentación del programa, el aspirante a La Moncloa ha explicado también que eliminará el Ministerio de Igualdad como departamento único, que quiere reformar la ley de la eutanasia y ha cuestionado que las chicas de 16 y 17 años aborten sin el conocimiento de sus padres. “¡Cómo no voy a ser feminista si me he criado en mi casa con muchas más mujeres que hombres!”, ha señalado. También ha puesto el foco en subir el salario medio como prioridad por encima del Salario Mínimo Interprofesional (SMI), y asegura que garantizará la “viabilidad” de las pensiones y que “reactivará el Pacto de Toledo” que regula el marco del sistema.</p><p><a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-23/feijoo-intentara-gobernar-aunque-no-sea-la-lista-mas-votada-mi-primer-objetivo-es-que-sanchez-se-vaya.html" target="_blank">Seguir leyendo</a></p>
sources.headline: Feijóo, dispuesto a “completar” la mayoría con Vox: “Mi primer objetivo es que Sánchez se vaya”

sources.body:
El president del PP, Alberto Núñez Feijóo , ha tret aquest divendres la bandera de l'ala més dura del partit: ha dit que reformarà la llei de l'eutanàsia , que reobrirà el debat sobre l' avortament i no ha volgut comprometre's a apujar el salari mínim interprofessional .

El popular és conscient que, si les xifres sumen, s'haurà d'entendre amb els de Vox per governar i ha aprofitat una entrevista a la SER per presentar les seves propostes més conservadores.

Feijóo ha assegurat que si és president del govern espanyol " obrirà el debat " perquè la societat reflexioni sobre si les menors de 16 anys poden interrompre el seu embaràs sense el consentiment familiar. Per ell, allò correcte seria que les adolescents hagin de compartir amb els seus pares aquesta "decisió vital, transcendent i irreversible".

Pel que fa l'eutanàsia, vol modificar la llei sobre la mort assistida per, entre altres aspectes, donar més pes a l'opinió de metges i especialistes.

Com han fet a les comunitats autònomes on el PP governa amb Vox, Feijóo vol suprimir també el Ministeri d'Igualtat , que s'integrarà en un altre departament, i assegura que això respon a la necessitat d'aprimar l'administració. Tot seguit, ha dit que es considera feminista perquè s'ha "criat a casa amb moltes més dones que homes".

Quan ha acabat l'entrevista, Sánchez ha publicat un missatge a X responent que Feijóo " és tan feminista que proposa carregar-se el ministeri d'Igualtat i retallar el dret de les dones a decidir sobre el seu propi cos". "Criar-se entre dones no et fa feminista. Defensar els seus drets, sí", ha afegit.

A diferència de les anteriors eleccions, on Feijóo demanava que governés la força més votada, ara s'obre a governar encara que no guanyi les eleccions , "tal com va fer Pedro Sánchez". "És un personatge tòxic i se l'ha de treure del govern", ha dit.

Fa uns dies Feijóo va fer públiques algunes de les seves propostes electorals mitjançant un document anomenat "Contracte amb Espanya". En aquest text es comprometia a incrementar "el salari mitjà" . Aquest divendres s'ha reafirmat en aquesta idea i ha evitat contestar si també apujarà el salari mínim interprofessional (SMI).

A més, ha carregat contra Sánchez a qui ha acusat de fer un "bon negoci" obligant les empreses a augmentar els sous perquè, d'aquesta manera, els treballadors cotitzen més IRPF . Poc després, la ministra de Treball, Yolanda Díaz, l'ha acusat de "mentir o no saber de què parla" perquè l'SMI no cotitza IRPF.

Pel que fa a les pensions , un camp de batalla durant aquesta precampanya, Feijóo ha volgut deixar clar que el seu partit garantirà el sistema reactivant el pacte de Toledo i asseient "sindicats, patronal, partits polítics i govern" per tirar endavant un pla que asseguri la permanència de la guardiola de les pensions.
sources.headline: Feijóo assumeix un govern amb Vox i diu que reformarà la llei de l'eutanàsia i obstaculitzarà l'avortament
